analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal law requiring prevailing-area wages on federally funded construction projects.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage law died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act, passed in 1931, requires contractors on federally financed construction of buildings and public works to pay workers the wage that prevails locally for their trade. The Copeland Act requires the Labor Department to police contractors' wage records on those jobs. This bill would repeal both laws, letting federal construction contractors pay whatever they choose. It was introduced by Rep. Ron Paul with 4 Republican cosponsors, referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, and sent to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, where it died without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Government construction contractors and subcontractors would gain, because labor is typically one of their largest costs and they could bid on federal projects while paying less than the local prevailing wage. Nonunion contractors in particular could underbid competitors who pay prevailing rates.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the Davis-Bacon Act, which requires the locally prevailing wage to be paid to laborers and mechanics on federally financed construction of public buildings and public works.
It repeals the Copeland Act's requirement that the Secretary of Labor regulate contractors and subcontractors on those federal construction projects, removing federal wage-record oversight.
The repeal would take effect 30 days after enactment but would not disturb contracts already in existence or bids already outstanding.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally funded projects would bear the cost, since contractors would no longer be required to pay the local prevailing wage on those jobs. Nonunion workers and minority- and apprentice-heavy trades would lose the wage floor most directly, and compliant contractors could see lower-wage rivals win federal bids.

drawbacks.text: Repealing Davis-Bacon removes the only wage floor on federally funded construction, and research on suspensions of the law (such as after Hurricane Katrina) has found workers on those jobs were paid substantially less; supporters would have to acknowledge that savings could come partly out of construction workers' paychecks.

The bill repeals the Copeland Act's contractor-regulation and recordkeeping requirements along with the wage floor, so even any replacement wage rules left to other statutes would lack the dedicated federal oversight mechanism this law provided.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Contractors and taxpayers who fund construction could see lower bids if contractor labor costs fall, but the clearest, most direct effect is lower pay for the construction workers on those federal jobs, and the bill offered no offsetting protection for them. The savings would flow to firms bidding on federal work; the cost would fall on the workforce building it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended, never reaching a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Paul introduced the bill on February 11, 1999, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
On March 5, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action was taken before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federally funded projects kept the prevailing-wage floor and the federal recordkeeping oversight, because the bill never advanced. Contractors who might have cut wages on federal jobs lost the opportunity.

for.name: Rep. Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon and Copeland Acts.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee and never took it up for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only a Republican sponsor and 4 Republican cosponsors and never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists; its fate was decided by committee inaction rather than a recorded division.

industries.note: Repeal would let contractors on federally funded projects pay below the local prevailing wage, cutting their largest cost. The gain comes directly out of construction workers' pay on public jobs.

Prevailing-wage rules are a core protection for union-scale and apprentice-heavy trades on public work. Repeal would expose their members to wage competition from lower-paying contractors on federal jobs.
